sports.name: Badminton
sports.description: Badminton is played indoors with a feather or nylon shuttle in singles, doubles and mixed doubles. Amateur events in India run from club and corporate tournaments to district, state and BAI ranking events, including Masters age groups from 35+. From 4 January 2027 the BWF default scoring changes to best of three games to 15 points.

level_definitions.advanced: You compete often at district, state or ranking level, choose shots tactically and can play several full matches in a day.

method: 1. Read the event category and map it to a tier (beginner, intermediate or advanced) using tier_rules.
2. For each number input: norm = clamp((value - floor) / (target[tier] - floor), 0, 1). Targets are listed per tier on each input.
3. For each choice input: norm = the points value of the chosen option (0 to 1).
4. base = sum(weight x norm) over all weighted inputs. Weights add up to 100.
5. Apply category_fit: hard gates force the verdict 'Not this one' whatever the score; soft adjustments are added to base.
6. score = round(clamp(base + adjustments, 0, 100)). Pick the verdict band that contains the score.
7. Apply caps from category_fit (a cap lowers the verdict to the named band if it is higher).

8. Gap advice: for every weighted input with norm < 0.6, compute lost = weight x (1 - norm); show the advice text for the 3 inputs with the largest lost points, largest first. Then add any fit or date messages.
9. Date: weeks_to_event = floor((event_date - today) / 7). If the event date is before today, do not show a verdict. Use date_rules to pick the extra line.
Badminton note: the longest_continuous_play_min target for the tier is multiplied by (1 + 0.5 x (planned_events - 1)) before step 2.

event_day_load.matches_per_day: 1 per event per day at multi-day BAI events (the 2025 Masters Nationals ran one round per day per event), so up to 3 a day if you enter singles, doubles and mixed. event_day_load.match_duration_min: About 17-40 minutes per match in research data; elite men's singles average about 31 minutes and women's singles about 23 minutes. Amateur doubles are usually 20-35 minutes.
event_day_load.intensity: Average heart rate above 90% of maximum in elite matches; typical rally about 7 seconds with 15 seconds rest, so about 31% of match time is active play.
event_day_load.scoring: Until 3 January 2027: best of 3 games to 21. From 4 January 2027 (BWF): best of 3 games to 15, 20-all then the 21st point wins, 60-second interval when the leader reaches 8, 120 seconds between games.

event_day_timeline.step: Check the draw and order of play (BAI draws are often made at the venue a day before). Note your first match number, court and time; pack your kit.
Eat your main pre-match meal and start sipping water.
Arrive at the venue and report to the control desk. Confirm your name in the draw and the reporting rules: missing your call can mean a walkover.
Find your court and listen to the announcement system; check how far behind schedule the matches are running.
Off-court warm-up for 15-20 minutes: easy jog, dynamic mobility, shadow footwork to all four corners, a few explosive lunges.
Small snack or sips of sports drink, re-grip if needed, put on fresh socks, keep warm.
At the court: toss, short knock-up as allowed by the umpire, then play. Use the mid-game and between-game intervals to drink and towel off.
Sign the score sheet if asked, report the result, and check when your next match is.
Refuel and rehydrate based on the gap to your next match; keep moving lightly so you do not stiffen.

nutrition_hydration: Plan for each match being 20-40 minutes of near-maximal effort: heart rate averages over 90% of maximum in elite matches, so treat a 3-match day like a long training session.

Eat a carbohydrate-based meal 3-4 hours before your first match (for example poha, 3 idlis with sambar, or rice with dal) and a small snack 60-90 minutes before (a banana or 3-4 dates). Avoid heavy fried food on the day.
Once your total playing time passes about an hour, take 30-60 g of carbohydrate per hour of play (USTA guidance). 500 ml of a 6% sports drink gives about 30 g; a medium banana gives about 25 g.

Weigh yourself before and after your first match. Each 1 kg lost is roughly 1 litre of sweat. The ACSM aims to keep losses under 2% of body weight (1.4 kg for a 70 kg player), so drink more in the next match if you lost more.

Replace salt as well as water on hot or humid days: ORS, salted nimbu pani or chaas all help (NCDC). A quarter teaspoon of salt contains about 590 mg of sodium (USTA). Plain water alone after heavy sweating can dilute blood sodium.

Between matches: under 1 hour, sip a sports drink or eat a banana only; 1-2 hours, a light snack such as 2 idlis, a peanut chikki or curd with fruit; over 2 hours, a small meal like curd rice or chapati with dal, finished at least 90 minutes before you play.
After your last match, drink about 1.5 litres for every kg of body weight lost over the next few hours, with a salty meal containing carbohydrate and protein.
Skip alcohol, very sugary soft drinks and large amounts of tea or coffee on hot match days. The NCDC heat advisory notes they can increase fluid loss or cause stomach cramps.
safety: Heatstroke is an emergency: stop play and call 108 if a player becomes confused, staggers, faints, has hot dry skin or a body temperature of 40 C or more. Cool them at once by moving them to shade, pouring cold water over large areas of skin and fanning (NCDC heat advisory).
Painful muscle spasms after long play in heat are heat cramps: rest in a cool place and drink ORS. Get medical help if they last more than an hour (NCDC).

If you have come from a cooler city or are returning after a break, build up exposure to heat gradually over 10-15 days before a hot tournament (NCDC). People with heart disease or high blood pressure are at higher risk and should check with a doctor first.
Many Indian halls are not air-conditioned. In April to June, check the forecast and bring extra fluids; humid halls raise sweat loss even when the temperature looks moderate.
Sweat on the court floor causes slips: ask the umpire to stop play and wipe the wet patch before the next rally.
Lunges and jumps load the ankle, knee and Achilles tendon. Warm up properly and stop if you feel a sudden pop or sharp pain at the back of the heel.
In doubles, keep your racket up at the net and agree with your partner who takes shots down the middle to avoid racket clashes.
If you are over 35 and new to competitive play, or have heart or blood pressure problems, get a medical check-up before a multi-match day.
beginner_tips: Scoring basics: every rally wins a point. Until 3 January 2027 most events play best of 3 games to 21 (at 20-all you need a 2-point lead, capped at 30). From 4 January 2027 the BWF default is games to 15, with the 21st point winning at 20-all. Check the prospectus.

The server serves from the right court when their score is even and from the left when it is odd. The shuttle must be hit below the server's waist line set in the Laws; ask the umpire which service rule the event uses.
Report on time and stay within earshot of announcements. If you are not at the court when called, the referee can award a walkover.
Test the shuttle with the umpire before the match and agree on a shuttle change if it gets damaged; do not change shuttles repeatedly to delay play.
When there are no line judges, call lines on your side honestly and give the benefit of the doubt to your opponent.
Shake hands with your opponent and the umpire after the match, win or lose.
In your first tournament, enter one event. You will learn the routine without being overloaded.
training_principles: Train in the work-rest pattern of matches: badminton rallies last about 7 seconds with about 15 seconds of rest, so use interval drills like 8 seconds of shadow footwork, 15 seconds of rest, repeated in sets.
Footwork first: most points are lost by being late to the shuttle. Two short footwork sessions a week improve every shot.
Increase training load in small steps, for example 10-15 minutes more court time per week, and keep at least one full rest day.
Play matches against slightly better players at least once a week; match play builds decision-making that drills do not.
Strengthen legs and core twice a week (squats, lunges, calf raises, planks) to protect knees and ankles.
Reduce training volume in the last week before the event so you start the day fresh.

sports.name: Tennis
sports.description: Tennis is played outdoors in India on hard and clay courts, in singles and doubles. Amateur options include club ladders, corporate and NTRP-style level events, veterans age groups and AITA ranking tournaments for juniors (U-12 to U-18) and adults. Matches usually last 60-90 minutes, so heat and back-to-back matches are the main event-day challenges.

level_definitions.beginner: You can rally at moderate pace and serve the ball in, but you have little control of depth or direction in a match.
level_definitions.intermediate: You hit with direction and some depth, come to the net when the chance is there, and play matches regularly.
level_definitions.advanced: You use pace, spin and tactics deliberately, handle hard-hit balls, and compete in ranking or open events.

event_day_timeline.step: Check the draw, order of play and scoring format (full sets or match tie-break). Check the weather and pack ice and fluids.
Main pre-match meal; start sipping fluids with some salt.
Arrive and sign in at the tournament desk. Late sign-in can mean a default.
Off-court warm-up for 15 minutes: jog, dynamic stretches, side shuffles, shadow swings.
Small snack or sports drink; check rackets, grips and fluids; apply sunscreen.
On-court: spin for serve, then the warm-up (usually 5 minutes). Agree on the scoring format and line-calling rules if there is no umpire.
Every changeover: drink, take some carbohydrate after the first hour, and put an ice towel on your neck in heat.
Report the score to the desk with your opponent, then cool down and start refuelling for your next match.

nutrition_hydration: Plan for 60-90 minutes per match in the sun. Carbohydrate stores can drop significantly after 60-90 minutes of intense singles (USTA), so start fuelling at changeovers from the first set.

Eat a carbohydrate-based meal 3-4 hours before your first match (for example poha, 3 idlis with sambar, or rice with dal) and a small snack 60-90 minutes before (a banana or 3-4 dates). Avoid heavy fried food on the day.
Once your total playing time passes about an hour, take 30-60 g of carbohydrate per hour of play (USTA guidance). 500 ml of a 6% sports drink gives about 30 g; a medium banana gives about 25 g.

Weigh yourself before and after your first match. Each 1 kg lost is roughly 1 litre of sweat. The ACSM aims to keep losses under 2% of body weight (1.4 kg for a 70 kg player), so drink more in the next match if you lost more.

Replace salt as well as water on hot or humid days: ORS, salted nimbu pani or chaas all help (NCDC). A quarter teaspoon of salt contains about 590 mg of sodium (USTA). Plain water alone after heavy sweating can dilute blood sodium.

Between matches: under 1 hour, sip a sports drink or eat a banana only; 1-2 hours, a light snack such as 2 idlis, a peanut chikki or curd with fruit; over 2 hours, a small meal like curd rice or chapati with dal, finished at least 90 minutes before you play.
After your last match, drink about 1.5 litres for every kg of body weight lost over the next few hours, with a salty meal containing carbohydrate and protein.
Skip alcohol, very sugary soft drinks and large amounts of tea or coffee on hot match days. The NCDC heat advisory notes they can increase fluid loss or cause stomach cramps.
safety: Heatstroke is an emergency: stop play and call 108 if a player becomes confused, staggers, faints, has hot dry skin or a body temperature of 40 C or more. Cool them at once by moving them to shade, pouring cold water over large areas of skin and fanning (NCDC heat advisory).
Painful muscle spasms after long play in heat are heat cramps: rest in a cool place and drink ORS. Get medical help if they last more than an hour (NCDC).

If you have come from a cooler city or are returning after a break, build up exposure to heat gradually over 10-15 days before a hot tournament (NCDC). People with heart disease or high blood pressure are at higher risk and should check with a doctor first.

For outdoor tennis in India, avoid playing in direct sun between 12:00 and 15:00 where you can (NCDC advisory) and ask the organiser about morning or evening slots. Humidity above about 70% on the coast (Mumbai, Chennai, Kochi) slows sweat evaporation, so you heat up faster at the same temperature.
Use the pro tour's heat rule as a guide: when WBGT reaches about 30 C, take extra cooling breaks; above 32 C, stop playing until it is cooler.
Hard courts get much hotter than the air temperature; check that your shoes have enough cushioning and change socks between matches.
Shoulder and elbow pain often comes from playing many matches without enough rest; stop if you feel sharp pain when serving.
beginner_tips: Scoring basics: points go 15, 30, 40, game; at 40-40 (deuce) you need two points in a row, unless the event uses no-ad scoring, where the next point wins. A set is first to 6 games by 2, with a tie-break at 6-6.
Many amateur events replace the third set with a 10-point match tie-break (first to 10, win by 2). Check before you start.
Without an umpire, you call the lines on your side. Call the ball out only if you clearly see space between the ball and the line; any doubt goes to your opponent.
Announce the score before each first serve so there is no argument later.
If a ball rolls onto your court during a point, call 'let' at once and replay the point.
Do not walk behind a court while a point is being played; wait for the end of the point.
Bring your own balls for warm-up and arrive early: late sign-in can mean losing by default.
training_principles: Most amateur matches are decided by serve and return; spend a quarter of practice time on them.
Train for 60-90 minutes of play with bursts: interval runs of 10-20 seconds hard, 20-30 seconds easy match the stop-start nature of points.
Play at the time of day your event is scheduled so your body gets used to the heat.
Increase match play gradually and keep at least one full rest day a week to protect the shoulder and elbow.
Add two short strength sessions a week (legs, core, shoulder external rotation) to reduce injury risk.

sports.name: Pickleball
sports.description: Pickleball is a paddle sport played on a badminton-sized court, mostly in doubles. In India, events sanctioned by the India Pickleball Association feed into the DUPR rating system, and most amateur draws are split by DUPR band and by age groups such as 35+ and 50+. Games are usually to 11 points, so a tournament day is many short games.

method: 1. Read the event category and map it to a tier (beginner, intermediate or advanced) using tier_rules.
2. For each number input: norm = clamp((value - floor) / (target[tier] - floor), 0, 1). Targets are listed per tier on each input.
3. For each choice input: norm = the points value of the chosen option (0 to 1).
4. base = sum(weight x norm) over all weighted inputs. Weights add up to 100.
5. Apply category_fit: hard gates force the verdict 'Not this one' whatever the score; soft adjustments are added to base.
6. score = round(clamp(base + adjustments, 0, 100)). Pick the verdict band that contains the score.
7. Apply caps from category_fit (a cap lowers the verdict to the named band if it is higher).

8. Gap advice: for every weighted input with norm < 0.6, compute lost = weight x (1 - norm); show the advice text for the 3 inputs with the largest lost points, largest first. Then add any fit or date messages.
9. Date: weeks_to_event = floor((event_date - today) / 7). If the event date is before today, do not show a verdict. Use date_rules to pick the extra line.

Team arrives; captain reports to the organiser desk, submits the squad list and IDs, and checks the first pitch.
Team warm-up for 20 minutes: jog, dynamic stretches, passing, short sprints and a few shots.
Final team talk; confirm substitution rotation; fill bottles and keep them at the pitch side.
Kick-off. Rotate substitutes early in hot conditions rather than waiting for tired players to ask.

nutrition_hydration: Plan for repeated sprints across several short matches: total playing time in a 5-a-side day can pass 90 minutes, which is a full-match workload in heat on turf.

Eat a carbohydrate-based meal 3-4 hours before your first match (for example poha, 3 idlis with sambar, or rice with dal) and a small snack 60-90 minutes before (a banana or 3-4 dates). Avoid heavy fried food on the day.
Once your total playing time passes about an hour, take 30-60 g of carbohydrate per hour of play (USTA guidance). 500 ml of a 6% sports drink gives about 30 g; a medium banana gives about 25 g.

Weigh yourself before and after your first match. Each 1 kg lost is roughly 1 litre of sweat. The ACSM aims to keep losses under 2% of body weight (1.4 kg for a 70 kg player), so drink more in the next match if you lost more.

Replace salt as well as water on hot or humid days: ORS, salted nimbu pani or chaas all help (NCDC). A quarter teaspoon of salt contains about 590 mg of sodium (USTA). Plain water alone after heavy sweating can dilute blood sodium.

Between matches: under 1 hour, sip a sports drink or eat a banana only; 1-2 hours, a light snack such as 2 idlis, a peanut chikki or curd with fruit; over 2 hours, a small meal like curd rice or chapati with dal, finished at least 90 minutes before you play.
After your last match, drink about 1.5 litres for every kg of body weight lost over the next few hours, with a salty meal containing carbohydrate and protein.
Skip alcohol, very sugary soft drinks and large amounts of tea or coffee on hot match days. The NCDC heat advisory notes they can increase fluid loss or cause stomach cramps.
safety: Heatstroke is an emergency: stop play and call 108 if a player becomes confused, staggers, faints, has hot dry skin or a body temperature of 40 C or more. Cool them at once by moving them to shade, pouring cold water over large areas of skin and fanning (NCDC heat advisory).
Painful muscle spasms after long play in heat are heat cramps: rest in a cool place and drink ORS. Get medical help if they last more than an hour (NCDC).

If you have come from a cooler city or are returning after a break, build up exposure to heat gradually over 10-15 days before a hot tournament (NCDC). People with heart disease or high blood pressure are at higher risk and should check with a doctor first.

For outdoor football in India, avoid playing in direct sun between 12:00 and 15:00 where you can (NCDC advisory) and ask the organiser about morning or evening slots. Humidity above about 70% on the coast (Mumbai, Chennai, Kochi) slows sweat evaporation, so you heat up faster at the same temperature.
Use WBGT where the organiser has a meter: FIFPRO recommends cooling breaks from about 26-28 C WBGT and moving matches above 32 C; FIFA makes cooling breaks mandatory above 32 C.
Remove all jewellery before playing; the Laws ban it and taping over it is not allowed.
Clean turf burns with water and antiseptic straight away; they get infected easily in heat.
Ankle sprains and hamstring strains are the most common injuries in small-sided games: warm up fully and do not play on through a sprain.
beginner_tips: Read the event rules before you arrive: 5-a-side often has a head-height rule (no passes or shots above head height) and a goalkeeper area that outfield players cannot enter.
Rolling substitutions are usually allowed in 5s and 7s: the player coming off must leave the pitch before the substitute enters.
Scoring and standings: group stages usually give 3 points for a win and 1 for a draw, then goal difference. Check how ties in knockouts are decided (often penalties).
Only the captain should speak to the referee; arguing over calls wastes time and can earn cards.
Be at your pitch before the scheduled time: many organisers award the match to the other team if you are not ready.
Shake hands with the other team and the referee after each match.
training_principles: Train for repeated sprints, not just long runs: small-sided football is short bursts with brief recoveries.
Play small-sided games in training with your actual team to build understanding and passing patterns.
Build training load gradually, and include hamstring and groin strength work (for example Nordic curls and Copenhagen planks) twice a week.
Do your harder sessions at the time of day your tournament matches are scheduled to adapt to the heat.
Cut back training in the last few days before the tournament so legs are fresh.

Find a practice table if available and hit forehands, backhands and serves for 10 minutes.
At the table: racket check if requested, 2-minute knock-up, choose serve or end, then play.
Use the short interval to towel off, drink and plan your next serve choices.
Sign the score sheet, report to the desk, check your next match and refuel lightly.

nutrition_hydration: Matches are short (about 10-25 minutes) but frequent, so total playing time across a group stage and knockouts can pass 2 hours. Eat little and often rather than one big meal.

Eat a carbohydrate-based meal 3-4 hours before your first match (for example poha, 3 idlis with sambar, or rice with dal) and a small snack 60-90 minutes before (a banana or 3-4 dates). Avoid heavy fried food on the day.
Once your total playing time passes about an hour, take 30-60 g of carbohydrate per hour of play (USTA guidance). 500 ml of a 6% sports drink gives about 30 g; a medium banana gives about 25 g.

Weigh yourself before and after your first match. Each 1 kg lost is roughly 1 litre of sweat. The ACSM aims to keep losses under 2% of body weight (1.4 kg for a 70 kg player), so drink more in the next match if you lost more.

Replace salt as well as water on hot or humid days: ORS, salted nimbu pani or chaas all help (NCDC). A quarter teaspoon of salt contains about 590 mg of sodium (USTA). Plain water alone after heavy sweating can dilute blood sodium.

Between matches: under 1 hour, sip a sports drink or eat a banana only; 1-2 hours, a light snack such as 2 idlis, a peanut chikki or curd with fruit; over 2 hours, a small meal like curd rice or chapati with dal, finished at least 90 minutes before you play.

If you have come from a cooler city or are returning after a break, build up exposure to heat gradually over 10-15 days before a hot tournament (NCDC). People with heart disease or high blood pressure are at higher risk and should check with a doctor first.
Many halls in India are not air-conditioned; in summer, check ventilation and drink to a plan rather than waiting for thirst.
Barriers and neighbouring tables are close: watch where you step when chasing wide balls.
Shoulder and lower-back strain come from many loops in a short time; warm up the shoulder and trunk properly.
Wipe sweat off the floor near your table before it causes a slip.
If you are over 35 and new to competition, or have heart or blood pressure problems, get a medical check before a long tournament day.
beginner_tips: Scoring basics: games are to 11, and at 10-all you need a 2-point lead. Matches are usually best of 5 games. Service changes every 2 points, and every point from 10-all.
Serve legally: rest the ball on an open palm, toss it at least 16 cm up without spin, and hit it as it falls, from behind the end line and above the table, keeping it visible to the receiver.
In doubles, partners must hit alternately and the serve goes diagonally from the right half to the right half.
Arrive when your group is called; the referee may give a walkover if you are absent.
Do not walk behind a table during a rally; wait for the point to end.
Shake hands with your opponent and the umpire after the match.
training_principles: Serve and receive practice gives the best return: spend 20% of practice time on it.
Use multiball and irregular drills so you learn to react to spin and placement changes, not just fixed patterns.
Train footwork in short, sharp sets of 10-20 seconds with full rest, matching rally lengths.
Play many different opponents, including left-handers and players with long pimples or defensive styles.
Strengthen legs, core and shoulders twice a week to protect the back and shoulder.

sports.name: Squash
sports.description: Squash is an indoor racket sport played in a four-walled court, almost always as singles. In India, the Squash Rackets Federation of India runs a star-rated national circuit with junior age groups from U-9 to U-19, open and masters categories, and clubs run box leagues and open events. It is one of the most physically demanding racket sports per minute.

method: 1. Read the event category and map it to a tier (beginner, intermediate or advanced) using tier_rules.
2. For each number input: norm = clamp((value - floor) / (target[tier] - floor), 0, 1). Targets are listed per tier on each input.
3. For each choice input: norm = the points value of the chosen option (0 to 1).
4. base = sum(weight x norm) over all weighted inputs. Weights add up to 100.
5. Apply category_fit: hard gates force the verdict 'Not this one' whatever the score; soft adjustments are added to base.
6. score = round(clamp(base + adjustments, 0, 100)). Pick the verdict band that contains the score.
7. Apply caps from category_fit (a cap lowers the verdict to the named band if it is higher).

8. Gap advice: for every weighted input with norm < 0.6, compute lost = weight x (1 - norm); show the advice text for the 3 inputs with the largest lost points, largest first. Then add any fit or date messages.
9. Date: weeks_to_event = floor((event_date - today) / 7). If the event date is before today, do not show a verdict. Use date_rules to pick the extra line.

level_fit.how: user_rank = rank of the user's profile level (beginner 1, intermediate 2, advanced 3); tier_rank = rank of the category tier; d = user_rank - tier_rank.

event_day_load.matches_per_day: Most circuit and club events play one round per day per category over several days, with plate draws giving losers extra matches; expect 1-2 matches a day, sometimes 3 on finals day (StartLine estimate).
event_day_load.match_duration_min: Elite men's matches average about 54 minutes with about 1.8 km covered; amateur best-of-5 matches are commonly 30-60 minutes.
event_day_load.intensity: Very high: elite players average about 92% of maximum heart rate during matches. Measured sweat rates in elite training average about 1.1 litres per hour.
event_day_load.scoring: Point-a-rally to 11, 2 clear at 10-all; best of 5 (sometimes 3). Warm-up up to 4 minutes (change sides after 2), up to 1 minute before play, 2 minutes between games.
